name: Numanggang
confidence_why: Hynum's 2001 phonology data sheet, the only first-hand description of Numanggang, calls stress contrastive and gives two minimal pairs, but Pennington 2014, describing the related language Ma Manda, argues from one of those pairs and without any Numanggang recordings that stress is instead weight-driven from a default initial syllable as in the other Erap languages.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog codes Numanggang lexical (contrastive, position unpredictable) on the strength of Hynum's 2001 OPD sentence 'Stress is contrastive' plus two pairs. Pennington cites that same sentence and disputes its interpretation: he reads the túo/tuót pair as a predictable weight-driven shift from default initial stress, which is a different type (weight-sensitive with initial default) rather than a lexical contrast. The disagreement is secondary-source reinterpretation, not new Numanggang data: Pennington had no recordings, examined only one of Hynum's two pairs, and the second pair (both syllables closed, the stressed-final form a verb inflection) is not explained by his weight account. So…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pennington does not describe Numanggang first-hand. He reports Hynum's (2001:3) claim that Numanggang stress is contrastive and then reanalyses Hynum's one cited pair (túo 'firstborn son' vs tuót 'enough') as a heavy (closed) second syllable attracting stress away from a light initial syllable, i.e. the same quantity-/quality-sensitive, default-initial pattern he sets up for Ma Manda (default word-initial stress; a heavy second syllable pulls stress rightward; vowel weight hierarchy /a/ > /e o/ > /ə/ > /i u/ > /ɨ/). He places Numanggang alongside Nek, Finongan, Uri and Nankina, all analysed as word-initial quality-sensitive systems. Footnote 27 (p. 92) admits he has no audio recordings of Numanggang, so the reanalysis rests on Hynum's printed examples only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on Numanggang. For Ma Manda he marks secondary stress (grave accent) on the final syllable of tri- and quadrisyllabic words in (25), p. 82-83, e.g. [qó.bɨ.sè] 'chicken', [də́.bu.ɡùm] 'star'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Numanggang. For Ma Manda he says the system is 'complicated and somewhat unreliable' (p. 81) and notes (23f) /lamut/ [lá.mut] 'poison', where a closed second syllable fails to attract stress, 'which contradicts the pattern' (p. 81). He does not address Hynum's other Numanggang pair (méŋ.giŋ 'eel' vs miŋ.gíŋ 'they gave him'), in which both syllables are closed and a weight account cannot decide.
new_statements.identity_note: Pennington 2014 is a phonology of Ma Manda (Glottolog sauk1252, ISO skc, also called Sauk), a neighbouring Erap language, not of Numanggang. Its Numanggang content is a two-sentence second-hand comment on Hynum's OPD (whose data are from the East/reference dialect, per the catalog's), plus scattered segmental comparisons (h-phoneme, epenthetic vocoid, loan adaptation, prenasalization). The same SIL e-Book is also held under sauk1252/ in the source-check tree, where it was read for Ma Manda itself.

readall_conflicts: One conflict, and it is about interpretation rather than data. The only first-hand source on Numanggang stress, Hynum's 4-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (2001/2004, held by the catalog), states 'Stress is contrastive' and gives two pairs (méŋ.giŋ 'eel' / miŋ.gíŋ 'they gave him'; túo 'first son' / tuót 'enough') with no default position; the catalog codes this lexical. Pennington 2014 (Ma Manda Phonology, pp. 81-82) quotes Hynum's claim and argues that the túo/tuót pair instead shows 'a heavy second syllable attracting the stress', i.e. the default-initial, weight- and quality-sensitive system he describes for Ma Manda and that has been proposed for the other Erap languages Nek, Finongan and Uri. Pennington's reanalysis is explicitly conjectural (no Numanggang audio, fn. 27), rests on one pair, and does not account for the méŋ.giŋ / miŋ.gíŋ pair, where both syllables are closed and the final-stressed member is an inflected verb. Neither source gives a rule statement for Numanggang beyond these two pairs. Hynum 1980 'A preliminary phonology of Numanggang' (ms, Ukarumpa, cited by Pennington with stress at pp. 25-29) would decide the question but is not open.
